q: Which statement about the ectopic ureter is FALSE?
o: In girls it can insert directly into the ovary
In a duplex system it drains the upper pole moiety
It can present as epididymitis in a young boy
In boys it most often ends in the posterior urethra
e: An ectopic ureter inserts only along Wolffian (mesonephric) derivatives; it reaches the fallopian tube, uterus, upper vagina or urethra only by rupturing into them, never the ovary. In girls the orifice lies anywhere from bladder neck to perineum, or in vagina, uterus or rectum, so a toilet-trained girl with continuous leakage despite normal voiding needs evaluation. In boys it always opens above the external sphincter (no incontinence): posterior urethra, vas, seminal vesicle or ejaculatory duct, never the anterior urethra. Ultrasound shows a tortuous dilated ureter (look for a ureterocele too); a tiny, poorly functioning moiety may be seen only on CT or MRI. Septic child with massive dilatation: temporary end ureterostomy. After upper pole heminephrectomy the stump is rarely a problem. A functioning upper pole is preserved by ureteropyelostomy or distal ureteroureterostomy (no data favour either).
s: Ch 41 Ectopic ureter, ureterocele and ureteral anomalies

q: Which statement about immune cells and cytokines is FALSE?
o: Regulatory CD4 T cells inhibit adaptive responses
Th2 cytokines (IL-4, 5, 10, 13) blunt antitumour immunity
Neutrophils present antigen on MHC like macrophages
The macrophage is the first immune cell in BCG response
e: Neutrophils (PMNs) are cytotoxic innate cells but only macrophages ingest pathogens and present antigen on MHC. Innate immunity is rapid, recognises PAMPs (pathogen-associated molecular patterns) and has no memory; adaptive immunity adds specificity and memory; they work together. An antitumour response needs Th1 (driven by IL-12; IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF-α), which also clears viruses. Th2 cytokines in urine after BCG, and Th2 CD4 cells in tumours, predict worse bladder cancer outcome. CD8 T cells kill almost any target, including chemoresistant cells. B cells (named after the bursa of Fabricius) make antibodies and memory cells; anti-BCG antibodies probably speed BCG clearance and weaken its effect. Immunoediting: elimination, equilibrium, escape; clinical tumours have escaped.

q: Which statement about primary urethral cancer is FALSE?
o: Most male anterior urethral cancers are squamous
Corpus cavernosum invasion makes the tumour T3
The distal third of the female urethra can be excised
Prognosis of pendulous cancer depends on cell type
e: Pendulous urethral cancer prognosis depends on stage, not histology, and is better than bulbomembranous; low-stage tumours are often cured by excision (or radiotherapy) with penile preservation. Posterior and proximal tumours present later, with worse survival. Women have more adenocarcinoma (from Müllerian tissue, glandular metaplasia, Skene glands or urothelium, not Cowper glands); the three main female types are urothelial, squamous and adenocarcinoma; sex is not independently prognostic. Risk factors: chronic inflammation, leukoplakia, strictures, HPV; female diverticula (adenocarcinoma); not bacterial vaginosis. Female prognosis depends on stage; proximal tumours present advanced. AJCC 8: T2 = spongiosum or periurethral muscle, T3 = corpora cavernosa or anterior vagina; no T2a/T2b. The urethral epithelium becomes squamous (not glandular) in the fossa navicularis. Small distal female tumours: excision or radiation with or without chemotherapy; excising the distal two-thirds causes incontinence. Advanced, bulbar or proximal disease needs MRI staging and multimodal therapy (neoadjuvant chemotherapy, chemoradiation, cystectomy with urethrectomy); radiation alone is inadequate. Prophylactic inguinal dissection has no proven benefit; palpable invasive nodes are treated as metastatic (chemoradiation then surgical consolidation).

q: Which statement about intracorporeal lithotripsy is FALSE?
o: EHL tends to damage ureteral mucosa
Holmium lasers cause more retropulsion than ballistic
Start holmium at 0.6 J and 6 Hz, then raise frequency
Ballistic devices carry the lowest perforation risk
e: Ballistic lithotripsy causes the most retropulsion (2%–17% of ureteral stones); the holmium laser's weak shockwave causes little. Holmium works photothermally (vaporisation); 'paint' the stone; raise frequency in preference to pulse energy. It releases cyanide from uric acid stones, with no reported harm. EHL (electrohydraulic) creates a hydraulic shockwave and cavitation bubble, works in saline, but risks mucosal injury and perforation. Ultrasound makes the stone resonate and can generate heat. Combined ultrasonic-ballistic devices clear stones best.
s: Ch 94 Surgery for upper tract calculi

q: Which statement about bladder structure and urothelium is FALSE?
o: The GAG layer is the proven primary urothelial barrier
Urothelium releases ATP, NO and acetylcholine
Uroplakins and tight junctions keep the barrier intact
Uropathogenic E. coli trigger immunity through TLR4
e: There is no definite evidence that the GAG (glycosaminoglycan) layer is the primary barrier; uroplakins and tight junctions (both unique to urothelium) maintain it. Urothelium is slightly water-permeable, actively transports sodium, changes shape with filling, and releases NO, ATP, acetylcholine, substance P and prostaglandins that act on afferents and smooth muscle. Lamina propria myofibroblasts and interstitial cells link urothelium, nerves and detrusor. The body lies above the ureteral orifices; the base is trigone and bladder neck. Smooth muscle works over a wide length range, so an empty bladder has little space. Men have a complete smooth muscle ring at the bladder neck and denser adrenergic innervation there; women do not. Distension reduces wall blood flow, more so with poor compliance. The external sphincter (pelvic floor periurethral striated muscle plus intramural striated muscle) is horseshoe-shaped over the ventral urethra in women; the levator ani does not surround the ventral urethra in either sex.

q: Which statement about vaginal mesh complications is FALSE?
o: Retropubic trocars injure the bladder more than TOT
Urethral dilation suits obstruction after a mesh sling
'Erosion' is an incorrect term and should not be used
Infected sacrocolpopexy mesh needs complete removal
e: Dilation does not relieve sling obstruction and risks urethral extrusion; catheterisation or early loosening or division are used. Use exposure, extrusion and perforation instead of 'erosion'. Large pores (type I macroporous, over 75 μm; knitted monofilament polypropylene about 1500 μm) admit macrophages (50 μm) and allow ingrowth; small pores admit bacteria (1 μm) but not leukocytes; woven Marlex is stiff with high extrusion. Population data show no rise in pelvic or other cancers or autoimmune disease. Abandon the sling if the urethra is injured. Bladder injury: retropubic 4.8% vs transobturator 0.6%, seen with a 70° lens on a full bladder; any sling or anterior mesh (0.7%–3.5%) can perforate (rectum 0.15% posteriorly), so cystoscopy follows every sling. Remove enough mesh to fix the problem (never asymptomatic mesh); divide slings lateral to the urethra. Retention: division; exposure: excise to 1 cm beyond; pain: maximal vaginal removal (arms rarely). After revision re-exposure is near 0%. Prolapse mesh exposes more than slings; small exposures heal conservatively; pain is hardest. Sacrocolpopexy sutures come out vaginally, mesh rarely; abdominal removal is morbid. Male slings: transient retention usually settles (urodynamics if not); for AUS, divide and leave the sling. Perforations: endoscopic or open repair.

q: Which statement about transurethral prostate surgery is FALSE?
o: Bipolar TURP with saline avoids TUR syndrome
Venous bleeding is darker and settles on bladder filling
TUIP suits glands over 60 mL and removes adenoma
The median lobe is usually resected first
e: TUIP (transurethral incision of the prostate) is for small glands (generally under 30 mL), removes no tissue, causes no TUR syndrome and gives retrograde ejaculation in up to 37% (perhaps less if unilateral). TUR syndrome: absorbed non-sodium monopolar irrigant causes dilutional hyponatraemia (confusion, nausea, vomiting, visual change, hypertension, bradycardia); lower the irrigant (about 60 cm), control bleeding, stop, give furosemide and calculated hypertonic saline. Bipolar meta-analysis: one TUR syndrome prevented per 50 patients, transfusion RR 0.53, fewer capsular perforations and shorter operations; late complications similar. Persistent urgency after relief of long-standing obstruction: check PVR, reassure, antimuscarinic or β3 agonist if emptying is good. Trial medical therapy before surgery; choose by patient and surgeon factors; do not neglect antibiotic prophylaxis.
s: Ch 146 Endoscopic and minimally invasive BPH therapy

q: Which statement about ureteroceles is FALSE?
o: Intravesical lesions do better after endoscopic incision
After the newborn period UTI is the usual presentation
Smoking during pregnancy is an accepted risk factor
About 80% arise from the upper pole of a duplex kidney
e: Ureteroceles are commoner in girls (4:1) and almost only in white children; 10% are bilateral and about 50% have reflux. Prenatal hydronephrosis is now the commonest perinatal route to diagnosis. They can cause upper pole obstruction, lower pole or contralateral reflux, incontinence (especially caecoureteroceles with a patulous bladder neck) and, least often, bladder outlet obstruction. A caecoureterocele has its orifice in the bladder but extends into the urethra. On VCUG (voiding cystourethrography) early filling views are needed or it effaces (it may also evert and mimic a diverticulum); endoscopic appearance varies with filling. Endoscopic decompression: multiple punctures or a transverse full-thickness incision as close to the bladder floor as possible (less reflux); similar success. Puncture cannot correct trigonal deficiency. At open excision pass a large catheter antegrade to remove residual obstructing flaps. A prolapsed ureterocele (smooth interlabial mass) is first punctured. Cobra-head sign on urography = single-system ureterocele. Non-refluxing, draining upper pole: prophylaxis, observation and repeat ultrasound may suffice.
s: Ch 41 Ectopic ureter, ureterocele and ureteral anomalies

q: Which statement about immunotherapy in urological cancers is FALSE?
o: Dense CD8 infiltrates predict better outcome in RCC
Sipuleucel-T targets prostatic acid phosphatase
PD-1 on tumour CD8 T cells marks an exhausted state
Ipilimumab plus nivolumab beats sunitinib first line
e: In kidney cancer a dense CD8 infiltrate paradoxically predicts a worse prognosis despite an active adaptive response; in bladder cancer it predicts a better one. Chronic inflammation drives bladder cancer (schistosomiasis causes squamous carcinoma) and probably prostate cancer (linked to charred-meat toxins). Checkpoint molecules on tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes damp CD8 function; PD-1/PD-L1 blockade restores it, shrinking tumours in a minority (book lists 'LAG-4'; the molecule is LAG-3). Bladder: PD-1/PD-L1 blockade works second line (response 20%–25%; book says better PFS and OS; KEYNOTE-045 pembrolizumab improved OS, not PFS) and in cisplatin-ineligible first-line patients; PD-L1 expression may select responders (enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab is now first line, EV-302). Kidney: anti-PD-1 works second line; combined CTLA-4/PD-1 blockade improves PFS and OS over sunitinib. Prostate: weak monotherapy activity. BCG (innate and adaptive) is the prototype immunotherapy. Vaccines are well tolerated but give few responses; several phase III trials failed; only sipuleucel-T is approved (asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic metastatic CRPC).

t: Urethral recurrence and prostatic urethral cancer
q: Which statement about urethral recurrence after cystectomy is FALSE?
o: Delayed urethrectomy removes the meatus en bloc
Prostatic urethral involvement raises recurrence risk
A positive wash cytology needs biopsy confirmation
Recurrence is commoner after neobladder than conduit
e: Urethral recurrence (5%–10% after cystectomy) is commoner with cutaneous diversion than with neobladder. Male risk factors: prostatic urethral involvement, positive urethral margin, cutaneous diversion; female: bladder neck involvement and positive margin. Most surgeons proceed to neobladder if intraoperative urethral frozen section is negative. Non-invasive recurrence: transurethral resection plus intraurethral BCG, good prognosis; invasive recurrence: usually radical urethrectomy, and neobladder bowel can be reused for a cutaneous diversion. Urethral wash cytology detects early recurrence. Delayed urethrectomy removes the whole urethra including fossa navicularis to avoid distal recurrence; no routine inguinal dissection or penectomy. Primary prostatic urethral carcinoma: mucosal or lamina propria disease is managed with TURP and BCG; stromal invasion needs neoadjuvant chemotherapy and cystoprostatectomy with urethrectomy.

q: Which statement about SWL (shockwave lithotripsy) is FALSE?
o: General anaesthesia gives higher stone-free rates
Cystine and brushite are the most SWL-resistant stones
The primary renal insult from shockwaves is vascular
A high stone burden increases renal shockwave injury
e: Bioeffects are increased by age (children and the elderly), hypertension (perinephric haematoma) and reduced renal mass, not by stone burden. Most if not all kidneys show acute injury (63%–85% on imaging at 24 hours with the HM3), centred on ruptured small veins, arteries and glomerular capillaries. Low-energy pretreatment then ramping up attenuates injury. Generators: electrohydraulic (spark gap), electromagnetic, piezoelectric (microexplosive not adopted). Ultrasound targeting needs skill and cannot show ureteral stones. Pain relates to skin energy density and focal size, not stone composition. Breakage: spall, squeezing, shear, superfocusing, cavitation, dynamic fatigue (two basic forces: mechanical stress and cavitation collapse). Fragility, least to most: cystine, brushite, calcium oxalate monohydrate, hydroxyapatite, struvite, calcium oxalate dihydrate, uric acid. A stent reduces steinstrasse for stones over 20 mm.
s: Ch 94 Surgery for upper tract calculi
b: Injury: age, HTN, low renal mass

q: Which statement about the nerves of the lower urinary tract is FALSE?
o: Lumbar sympathetics excite the bladder neck and urethra
Silent C-fibre afferents can be recruited by disease
Pudendal nerves excite the detrusor and the sphincter
Bowel inflammation can sensitise the bladder
e: Pudendal (S2–S4, somatic) nerves excite only the external sphincter. Pelvic parasympathetics (S2–S4) excite the bladder and relax the urethra; lumbar sympathetics inhibit the body and excite base and urethra; all three carry afferents. Parasympathetic afferent-efferent links may exist in intramural ganglia. Pelvic afferents signal volume and contraction amplitude; nerve density is greatest at the bladder neck and proximal urethra. Bladder afferents are classed by receptive field and chemical sensitivity and vary by species; sensitisation opens terminal ion channels, releases inflammatory mediators, and develops quickly but is not easily resolved. Filling gives episodic bursts of sensation (Nathan); imminent micturition may be sensed in the urethra. Cross-organ sensitisation (bowel, uterus, urethra, vagina, prostate; e.g. IBS) may underlie chronic pelvic pain. Reduced afferent sensitivity (disease, ageing) can impair voiding.

t: Lasers and minimally invasive BPH therapy
q: Which statement about laser and minimally invasive BPH treatment is FALSE?
o: Prostatic urethral lift implants sit anterolaterally
HoLEP results rival open prostatectomy
Sham BPH procedures rarely change symptom scores
PVP on anticoagulation lengthens hospital stay
e: Sham arms (microwave thermotherapy, urethral lift trials) often show significant symptom and flow gains and are well tolerated. PUL (prostatic urethral lift) implants are anterolateral, avoiding posterolateral neurovascular bundles and anterior veins, and compress the transition zone; use when volume is under 80 g with no middle lobe. PUL and water vapour therapy spare erection and ejaculation, but durability is uncertain. Laser safety: eye protection for everyone including the patient, signs on doors, cover windows. PVP (photoselective vaporisation) is safe on anticoagulants (more irrigation and catheter time, not more transfusion). HoLEP has a steep learning curve, and morcellator injuries can be catastrophic. Thulium is newest, with limited data. Medical therapy and new technology have changed case mix; lasers are growing fastest.
s: Ch 146 Endoscopic and minimally invasive BPH therapy
b: PUL anterolateral; <80 g, no middle lobe

q: Which statement about ureteral duplication and anomalies is FALSE?
o: UPJ obstruction usually affects the lower pole
The upper pole orifice lies cranial and lateral
Duplex kidneys come from two separate ureteric buds
Retrocaval ureter is moved ventral to the vena cava
e: Weigert-Meyer rule: the upper pole orifice (incorporated later) lies caudal and medial to the lower pole orifice, and the ectopic ureter or ureterocele belongs to the upper pole. Lower pole problems mirror single-system disease (UPJ obstruction, reflux); upper pole problems reflect abnormal ureteral formation (ectopia, ureterocele). Duplex kidneys are often longer than normal. Do not separate duplex ureters distally (shared blood supply). Primary reflux results from a lateral orifice, short submucosal tunnel, poor trigone and abnormal orifice shape (not a lax bladder neck). Dysplasia reflects poor ureteric bud–blastema interaction. Triplicate ureter: commonest form is all three joining at one orifice. Retrocaval ureter (book: persistent lumbar subcardinal vein) needs division and ventral relocation. Fibroepithelial polyps are commonest at the UPJ (can occur anywhere); excise and do a dismembered pyeloplasty.
s: Ch 41 Ectopic ureter, ureterocele and ureteral anomalies
b: Weigert-Meyer: upper pole caudal and medial

q: Which statement about PCNL (percutaneous nephrolithotomy) is FALSE?
o: Overadvancing the sheath is the usual serious error
An upper pole puncture is a risk for colon injury
Supracostal access is done in full expiration
Puncture a posterior calyx through the avascular zone
e: Colon injury risk is with access lateral to the posterior axillary line, horseshoe kidney, kyphoscoliosis, jejunoileal bypass and thin women, not upper pole access. Absolute contraindications: uncorrected coagulopathy and untreated UTI. Prophylaxis: cephalosporin (S. epidermidis is the commonest secondary organism). Supracostal access suits upper calyceal stones, UPJ stricture needing endopyelotomy (aligns with the UPJ), multiple lower pole calyces, ureteral stones, staghorns with upper pole burden and horseshoe kidneys (not cystine stones as such). Use a hydrophilic wire and isotonic saline irrigation (avoids dilutional hyponatraemia). Horseshoe kidney: incomplete ascent, malrotation, anteromedial lower calyces, so use a more medial posterior upper or middle calyx. Haemorrhage is the main complication (transfusion under 1%–10%); embolisation for AV fistula or pseudoaneurysm in under 0.5% (about 1 in 200). Uncontrolled tract bleeding: clamp the tube, then Kaye tamponade balloon. Extraperitoneal colon injury: double-J stent and pull the nephrostomy back into the colon. Remove struvite completely.
s: Ch 94 Surgery for upper tract calculi
b: Colon risk: lateral to posterior axillary line

q: Which statement about bladder transmitters and receptors is FALSE?
o: M2 receptors act through inhibition of cAMP
Botulinum toxin blocks presynaptic vesicle fusion
M3 activation contracts the detrusor via IP3 and calcium
ATP is the main excitatory transmitter in normal humans
e: Acetylcholine is the main excitatory transmitter in the normal human detrusor; ATP (P2X and P2Y receptors) matters in overactivity and bladder pain. Most detrusor nerves contain acetylcholinesterase; NO and VIP are also released. Muscarinic M3: IP3 hydrolysis, intracellular calcium release, nifedipine-sensitive calcium influx and Rho-kinase. M2 (unique): lowers cAMP. β2 and β3 receptors raise cAMP and relax the detrusor; β3 agonists act at several sites for OAB; α1 mechanisms modulate reflex activity and blood flow. Urethral tone depends on α-adrenergic receptors and sympathetic input; parasympathetic NO is the main urethral relaxant during voiding. G-protein-coupled receptors mediate many functions and regulate intracellular calcium. Sympathetic preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine. Neuronal action potentials come from Na influx; resting potential needs energy (Na/K pump).

t: Ureteroscopy and stones in special situations
q: Which statement about ureteroscopy and stones in pregnancy is FALSE?
o: Pregnancy raises the rate of new stone formation
URS with holmium suits patients who stay anticoagulated
Ureteral avulsion: place a nephrostomy at once
A stent may be omitted after uncomplicated URS
e: Pregnancy causes absorptive hypercalciuria and mild hyperuricosuria, offset by more citrate, magnesium and urine volume, so new stone rates do not change (though stents encrust faster). 50%–80% of stones in pregnancy pass; transvaginal ultrasound shows the lower ureter. Most ureteral stones under 5 mm pass. URS prophylaxis: book says fluoroquinolone; FDA safety warnings and resistance now favour alternatives (e.g. cephalosporin or TMP-SMX). The rigid ureteroscope reaches the whole ureter more easily in women. Stricture after URS is 3%–6% (book), so image afterwards. A stone extruded outside the ureter: stop and stent.
s: Ch 94 Surgery for upper tract calculi

t: Storage, voiding reflexes and central control
q: Which statement about micturition reflexes and control is FALSE?
o: Central serotonergic activation facilitates voiding
PAG and pontine micturition centre form the switch
The guarding reflex increases sphincter activity
Normal compliance is both passive and neurally active
e: Central serotonergic activation suppresses voiding by inhibiting parasympathetic input. Storage relies on parasympathetic quiescence, sympathetic reflex negative feedback (outlet closure, inhibited contraction), urothelial signalling and low pressure below threshold. The guarding reflex: bladder or urethral afferents activate pudendal motor neurons, raising outlet resistance. Compliance is due to passive viscoelasticity plus active neural signalling. Cx43 (connexin-43) gap junctions couple detrusor cells and show circadian expression. The resting bladder may be spontaneously active. Switching to voiding can be reflex or voluntary; the urethra-to-bladder facilitatory reflex was described by Barrington. The dorsal pontine tegmentum (Barrington nucleus, PMC, M region) controls micturition through a spinobulbospinal reflex; without the switch, incontinence results. Limbic and social-propriety cortical circuits govern continence. Female continence: submucosal vascular cushion, guarding reflex, sympathetic tone and the hammock (fixed dorsal support allowing ventral compression).

q: Which statement about lower tract pathophysiology is FALSE?
o: Spinal injury unmasks a C-fibre bladder reflex
IC urine contains antiproliferative factor and ATP
Bladder capacity is what typically declines with age
Water avoidance stress models human BPS/IC best
e: With ageing, bladder sensation, contractility and urethral pressure decline. After spinal cord injury a C-fibre spinal reflex, NGF, detrusor GPCR activity and sphincter contractions drive neurogenic overactivity. Obstruction changes collagen subtypes, causes afferent and efferent neuronal hypertrophy and a C-fibre reflex, with denervation supersensitivity and CNS changes. Transgenic overactivity models: reduced BK channels and reduced β1-integrin. Isolated nocturia: nocturnal polyuria, sleep apnoea, peripheral oedema. SUI causes: poor urethral support, loss of urothelial seal, low sacral serotonin. Sex steroids influence bladder receptors and growth.

t: Muscle mechanics and how bladder therapies work
q: Which statement about detrusor mechanics and treatment mechanisms is FALSE?
o: The motor-sensory idea explains antimuscarinic urgency relief
Low Pdet voiding in women need not mean weak detrusor
Neuromodulation inhibits somatic afferent processing
Smooth muscle lacks actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling
e: Both smooth and striated muscle use actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling; only striated muscle has visible striations, and skeletal muscle lacks intermediate filaments. Some women void with little Pdet rise because Pdet is not the only measure of mechanical work. Sacral neuromodulation (effective for refractory OAB and non-obstructive retention via central modulation) acts by somatic inhibition of spinal sensory processing.
